title: Regional innovation: Network sequence matters more than volume
desc: Links novelty to open anchors, mobility and reciprocal institutional development while separating firm, regional and influence outcomes.

kps.k: Organisational novelty emerges through exchanges across institutional boundaries, not simply through technological replacement.
kps.d: The cluster explains biotechnology’s emergence through scientists, financiers and managers transferring practices among academic science, venture finance and commercial health care. Archival research and founder interviews underpin this account. These exchanges changed participants’ routines and identities rather than merely connecting otherwise unchanged organisations. The accounts differ in emphasis: Part IV Introduction stresses that new and old models commingled, while Chance, Nécessité, et Naïveté argues that collaborative research eventually supplanted closed industrial laboratories and entrenched academic disciplinary structures.

qs.q: Using historical analysis of archival materials, supplemented by interviews with DBF founders, Powell and Sandholtz piece together the “lash- up” process that melded elements from three separate realms—academic science, venture fi- nance, and commercial health care—into an in- teractively stable pattern.
qs.a: Part IV Introduction: Contemporary Capitalism and Science · Academia · 2012

qs.q: Over time, this approach supplanted the formerly dominant model of a large, inwardly focused, hermetically sealed industrial R&D lab, as well as the entrenched disciplinary structure of traditional biomedical departments at research universities.
qs.a: Chance, Nécessité, et Naïveté: Ingredients to Create a New Organizational Form · Academia · 2012

kps.k: Regional development depends on how diverse organisations interact, not on resource abundance alone.
kps.d: Powell, Packalen and Whittington compare eleven early US biotechnology regions using a Bioscan-based database covering 661 dedicated biotechnology firms worldwide and more than 3,000 partners during 1988–2004. Boston, the Bay Area and San Diego developed robust clusters despite substantial scientific and financial resources elsewhere. The authors attribute this divergence to community-oriented anchors connecting different organisational forms. In the 1990 comparison, one organisational type held 50–80 percent of ties in each nascent region except Los Angeles; the authors suggest that this dominance inhibited cross-domain mixing. The introductions summarise this same research rather than provide independent corroboration.

qs.q: To explore these and related questions, we built a database that includes 661 dedicated bio- technology firms worldwide, and the more than 3,000 partners with these firms, from 1988– 2004.
qs.a: Organizational and Institutional Genesis: The Emergence of High-Tech Clusters in the Life Sciences · Academia · 2012

qs.q: Our argument hinges on two main factors: one, the presence of a diversity of organizations, and two, connections mediated through anchor tenants, some of which prompted the bound- ary crossing we have termed transposition.
qs.a: Organizational and Institutional Genesis: The Emergence of High-Tech Clusters in the Life Sciences · Academia · 2012

kps.k: Open anchors, mobile careers and multiple independent connections can sustain exploration within a cohesive core.
kps.d: An Open Elite argues that cohesion makes exchange reliable while ties to diverse newcomers sustain exploration; neither feature suffices alone. Scientists’ cross-sector careers carry norms and practices as well as knowledge. Anchors need not be universities: research organisations, investors and biotechnology firms performed catalytic roles in different regions. The reported histories include Boston’s research institutions, Bay Area scientific and financial intermediaries, and Hybritech alumni founding interconnected San Diego firms. This explains openness in the cases examined, not a general tendency for incumbent elites to remain receptive.

qs.q: Thus, network cohesion and organizational diversity operate as countervailing forces, with the former enhancing the reliability of exchange and the latter pulling in newcomers that aid in exploration.
qs.a: An Open Elite: Arbiters, Catalysts, or Gatekeepers in the Dynamics of Industry Evolution? · Academia · 2012

qs.q: “An- choring diversity” refers to the mediating role of  community-oriented organizations—sometimes public research organizations, sometimes ven- ture capitalists, sometimes DBFs themselves—in the cores of each of the three successful clusters.

kps.k: Network development is sequential and reciprocal, leaving room for disagreement about causation.
kps.d: The biotechnology comparison suggests that established clusters built local ties before interregional and global partnerships; earlier external connections in nascent regions may have dampened local growth. This is not an argument against distant ties, which can complement local exchange and prevent intellectual isolation. Why the Valley Went First explicitly contrasts network-driven explanations of regional advantage with claims that technological trajectories and regional success produce networks. Fleming and colleagues propose reciprocal influence and longitudinal analysis. Its supplied excerpts introduce the inquiry; the introductions separately report earlier Silicon Valley aggregation and greater cross-industry mobility.

qs.q: Moreover, we find an intriguing suggestion of a “virtuous cycle” in the successful clusters: local ties were formed first, then connections were made to the other established clusters, then global linkages were created.
qs.a: Organizational and Institutional Genesis: The Emergence of High-Tech Clusters in the Life Sciences · Academia · 2012

qs.q: Turning the argument on its head, the skeptics propose that networks result from—and do not necessarily improve—regional innovative advantage (Feldman 2001).
qs.a: Why the Valley Went First: Aggregation and Emergence in Regional Inventor Networks · Academia · 2012

kps.k: Firm survival, regional growth and institutional influence are distinct outcomes.
kps.d: The authors argue that biotechnology’s organising principles spread into universities and large corporations even as dedicated firms declined in prevalence. They do not equate this decline with universal commercial failure: Chance, Nécessité, et Naïveté identifies Amgen, Biogen, Chiron and Genentech as scientific and commercial successes. Likewise, thriving regions did not generally confer lower firm failure rates; related analyses found no statistical difference except somewhat earlier failure in San Diego. Regional growth reflected formation exceeding dissolution. The practical analytical implication is to examine failed ventures and the persistence of their practices alongside surviving firms.

qs.q: In short, even though the science-based, dedicated biotech firm has declined in its prevalence, the organizing principles that DBFs created have spread to the most central members of the life sciences field, forming a new center of gravity.
qs.a: An Open Elite: Arbiters, Catalysts, or Gatekeepers in the Dynamics of Industry Evolution? · Academia · 2012

qs.q: Companies such as Amgen, Biogen, Chiron, and Genentech brought important novel medicines to market, developed different means for con- ducting research and clinical trials, and reaped considerable gains in the process.
qs.a: Chance, Nécessité, et Naïveté: Ingredients to Create a New Organizational Form · Academia · 2012

kps.k: Institutional flexibility enables hybrid practices but also changes public science.
kps.d: Academic Laboratories argues that academic patenting required adaptable understandings of invention and inventorship. Its Stanford counterfactual inquiry compares mechanisms behind changing laboratory patenting patterns, but the supplied material does not identify a winning mechanism. The authors suggest that more rigid university governance would have obstructed the circulation of practices. Across the cluster, boundary crossing works in both directions: companies adopt academic practices while universities adopt entrepreneurial ones. These hybrids can retain different standards of worth, and the regional study cautions that boundary crossing also transforms public institutions’ identities.

qs.q: The academic life sciences provide an important parallel as en- gagement in patenting as a new and contradic- tory form of disclosure required a requisite level of mutability in social and technical categories, such as invention and inventor, for emergence to take place.
qs.a: Academic Laboratories and the Reproduction of Proprietary Science: Modeling Organizational Rules through Autocatalytic Networks · Academia · 2012

qs.q: Moreover, these differ- ent organizational models operate according to different rules and registers of worth, even when they are engaged in similar activities.
qs.a: An Open Elite: Arbiters, Catalysts, or Gatekeepers in the Dynamics of Industry Evolution? · Academia · 2012

kps.k: The practical implications concern institution-building processes, not a transferable recipe for success.
kps.d: The research directs attention to cross-domain relationships, career mobility, anchor openness and the timing of local and distant connections rather than funding or co-location alone. However, the authors stress that starting conditions and sequences constrain outcomes, and catalytic opportunities may be brief. Biotechnology’s dependence on university science, intellectual property and public research funding limits straightforward generalisation. Information-technology comparisons suggest broader relevance, but neither those comparisons nor the Stanford modelling inquiry establish universal effects or justify overstating universities’ product-development capacity.

qs.q: We want to be careful that our argument is not perceived as a recipe for suc- cess.16 The account we are giving is very much a process story: starting points and sequences mat- ter; what types of organizations are involved and where you begin shape where you can go.
qs.a: Organizational and Institutional Genesis: The Emergence of High-Tech Clusters in the Life Sciences · Academia · 2012

qs.q: The last two chapters in this part move from the life sciences to information technology, sug- gesting the generality of cross-network refunc- tionality across contemporary high-technology industries.
qs.a: Part IV Introduction: Contemporary Capitalism and Science · Academia · 2012

vlens.an: The curated academia-and-research sources accept the proposition that regional innovation depends on the composition, mediation and development of networks rather than connection or resource volume alone, and collectively make material extensions to it. Their common explanation centres on organisational diversity joined by open anchor institutions, career mobility and cross-domain transfers of practices; comparative evidence also shows that regions with similar aggregate resources or network density can develop different levels and forms of connectivity. The strongest extension is processual: one longitudinal biotechnology study proposes that successful clusters formed local ties before interregional and global links, while the inventor-network work frames networks and regional advantage as reciprocal, co-evolving outcomes rather than a one-way causal relationship. Other sources add institutional flexibility, cohesive-but-diverse network cores, and the distinction among firm survival, regional growth and wider institutional influence. Material variation concerns evidential reach and emphasis. The regional biotechnology study directly develops the sequencing claim with comparative longitudinal data, whereas several introductions synthesise that same research rather than independently corroborate it. The supplied inventor-network excerpts establish a reciprocal framework and research design but do not report the results explaining Silicon Valley’s earlier aggregation. Other historical and network accounts strongly support boundary crossing, mobility and organisational hybridity but do not directly test whether sequence matters more than volume. The sources also caution that biotechnology’s institutional conditions limit generalisation and that these mechanisms should not be treated as a transferable policy recipe.

qs.q: Moreover, we find an intriguing suggestion of a “virtuous cycle” in the successful clusters: local ties were formed first, then connections were made to the other established clusters, then global linkages were created.
qs.a: Organizational and Institutional Genesis: The Emergence of High-Tech Clusters in the Life Sciences · Academia · 2012

qs.q: Surely networks influence regional advantage and are in turn shaped by regional suc- cess or failure.
qs.a: Why the Valley Went First: Aggregation and Emergence in Regional Inventor Networks · Academia · 2012

elens.an: The pre-2015 sources collectively accept the proposition that regional innovation depends on the structure, composition and development of networks rather than connection or resource volume alone, and they materially develop that account. Their common explanation centres on diverse organisational forms interacting through open anchor institutions, mobile careers and cross-domain transfers of practices; comparative evidence also indicates that similarly resourced or similarly dense regions can develop different connectivity and innovation outcomes. Material variation concerns emphasis and evidentiary reach: some sources provide longitudinal regional comparisons and propose a local-to-interregional-to-global sequence, while others focus on organisational hybridity, institutional flexibility, cohesive-but-diverse network cores, or the distinction between firm survival, regional growth and wider institutional influence. The inventor-network source further treats causation as reciprocal—networks shape regional advantage while regional outcomes reshape networks—and its supplied excerpts introduce the inquiry rather than report all results. Several sources caution that starting conditions matter and that biotechnology does not supply a universal policy recipe. This assessment applies only to the curated sources supplied, not to all pre-2015 scholarship.
